coauthors.name: Emanuel J. Jack
coauthors.bio: Rabbi Emanuel J. Jack (1890-1942), born in Rochester, New York, was a Reform movement rabbi and military chaplain in the United States. In 1908, he received his A.B. degree from the University of Chicago after which, in 1911, he was ordained by Hebrew Union College and in 1923, received an M.A. from Columbia University. Rabbi Jack first served as rabbi of Temple Emanu-El (Pueblo, Colorado), 1911-1917, and then at the Reform Temple (Stockton, California), 1917-1921. During World War Ⅰ, he became a chaplain with the American Expeditionary Forces. In 1921 Rabbi Jack came to Little Rock, Arkansas where he served as rabbi for Temple B'nai Israel (Little Rock, Arkansas) until 1926 when he became rabbi of Temple Emanu-El (Little Rock), until 1931 when he moved to New York. He was named a major in the Army Reserve in 1927 and national chaplain of the Veterans of Foreign Wars in 1931. In civic life, Rabbi Jack was a member of the California Motion Picture Censorship Board in 1920 and 1921 and was State chairman of the Arkansas Americanization Commission from 1922 to 1926. He became principal of the Yonkers Night High School from 1933 to 1935 and served as president of the Educational Advisers Association (New York, New Jersey and Delaware region). He was active in the so-called Good Fellowship Movement of English speakers internationally, and inaugurated a "Better Understanding Week" that was observed in Yonkers in 1929. On radio station WFAS, he served as rabbi of the Temple of Better Understanding (the Congregation of the Air). He had been editor and publisher of The Voice and editor of The Westchester Jewish Weekly. In 1936, Rabbi Jack brought suit in the Supreme Court in New York against Fritz Kuhn, then leader of the German-American Bund, for $3,000,000, charging that Kuhn had slandered the Jews in statements the former Bund leader was alleged to have made when he was a witness before a joint legislative committee of the State Senate. Rabbi Jack wrote plays and books including The Flag Speaks, The Unknown Soldier, Every American and Every Jew.

excerpt: This prayer of the guest chaplain was offered in the first month of the first session of the 69th US Senate, and published in the Congressional Record, vol. 67 part 1 (14 December 1925), page 762.
content:
Guest Chaplain: Rabbi Emanuel J. Jack, of Little Rock, Arkansas
Sponsor: n/a
Date of Prayer: 14 December 1925

Contribute a translation Source (English)
Universal power,
unending strength,
and source of inspiration,
unto Thee, O Thou Eternal One,
Thou who hast ever directed and guided
the work of Thy servants,
unto Thee, great Mind of the universe,
should ever be our first thought.
Gratefully do we acknowledge
our constant dependence upon Thee
and readily do we realize and recognize
the weakness and the vainness of human endeavor
without Thy gracious favor.
O great Guardian,
Thou who hast watched over our beloved country
from the very moment of its birth even unto now
and hast blessed it so beautifully and so bountifully,
humbly do we beseech Thee
to continue the great love and protection upon it,
upon its Chief Executive,
upon the Presiding Officer of this august assembly,
upon all its counselors,
and all who have been intrusted with the sacred charge
of promoting and protecting its national ideals.
Yea, even the highest heaven hearkeneth to Thy whispering,
and Thy glorious presence is displayed in all the extent of nature.
In the heavens above and on the earth beneath
Thy goodness is manifested in every respect,
and Thy greatness guardeth
and governeth
and guideth
all motion.
So, great Power,
sanctify all the work before this body.
May all assembled here be blessed
with strength and with understanding
and consecrate themselves thoroughly and completely
to the high purpose to which they have been called,
that of furthering to the utmost
the welfare and well-being
of these United States and all its citizenry.
And may the good thoughts which arise in the mind of any
be supported by the labors of many
and become fruitful and useful to the common interest of all,
bringing blessing to untold numbers
and glory to Thy name, O God.
Amen.

This prayer of the guest chaplain was offered in the first month of the first session of the 69th US Senate, and published in the Congressional Record, vol. 67 part 1 (14 December 1925), page 762.
